summary:
Review of rsi6/experiments/targets.py (REPO below is .../scratchpad/review1/repo, WORK is .../scratchpad/review1/work_a).

No blocking defect found. Four major findings: three in the checks before the unlock and on a second start, one in report.py (outside my part, raised because question 2 asks). The arms of process c and matched() implement their registered definitions, with small, conservative deviations from reading (d).

Answers to the five questions:

1. Arms. c:self is frozen_c[-1]["version"] with no memory; external.py:85-87 takes it from the last adopt record of process c, or generation 0 if there is none. c:frozen and c:skills are the same list objects as frozen and skills, and the dev target_done record has identical keys for them. c:compute and c:search are matched to cpu(c:self run) + spent_c / (targets x seeds); I recomputed every "reached" flag in the dev ledger and all 14 agree. spent_by_process_c counts each run once: every run purpose after registration_c in main.jsonl matches the pattern, none before it does, and the external gate (gate:c:external:...) and recursion (recursion:...) purposes do not match. Process c seeds are its own, so nothing is served from earlier processes and left out.

2. matched(). It stops only when no pair is pending or after 12 levels, and "reached" is then computed from the last record, so it cannot be wrong. No division by zero with the registered budgets (factor is at least 2, base budgets 40 and 1). No unbounded loop. With a flat CPU it runs 12 levels up to a budget of about 1e11 to 4e13 times nothing and records reached False. Deviations from reading (d) are listed as a minor finding. The matched record holds arm, keys, reached, share_per_run and the spend; that is enough for the report, but the report does not use it to void anything.

3. Restart. Runs are keyed and served from the ledger; the level sequence of matched() is a function of recorded CPU, so a second start recomputes the same budgets and keys (stub test: 0 new runs). The memory is reproducible across processes: I repeated the forecasting and jobshop acquisitions (11.6 CPU-s) and the recomputed key of target:skills binpacking 301 is the one in the dev ledger, with no record appended. Weak points: matched and target_done are appended again on every start, replace is written before validation, and the list recorded at the unlock is never compared again.

4. Checks. On a ledger that holds registration_c the test refuses until the freeze of c and the external gate are recorded (tested on a 3400-record prefix of main.jsonl). On a copy that ends before registration_c it passes and unlocks. The list checks are weak (three findings). --dev refuses main.jsonl and live.jsonl and never writes an unlock, so the role lock still refuses a target category on a scratch ledger; --dev 0 is the exception.

5. Fairness. All arms use the same seeds (301 to 308), the same run budget and the same fresh instances. Memory is used only by skills, memory, b:skills, b:memory, c:skills (alias) and c:memory. "earlier" is every category in the source pool now except the targets, which makes the memory depend on whether the external gate ran. The dev run shows the memory arms collapsing and the search arm insensitive to its budget; both are behaviour of the frozen learner, reported as notes.

Compute used: about 15 CPU-seconds, one process at a time. No learner run on any target or reserve category; target adapters were never loaded in my tests (environments.load was stubbed). Nothing under REPO was modified; scripts and ledger copies are in WORK.
checks_run: Read targets.py in full, plus kernel/run.py, kernel/roles.py, kernel/ledger.py, meta/rounds.py, learner/learner.py lines 384-639, report.py lines 180-247 and 300-317, and the relevant lines of external.py, recursion.py and alternating.py
Read registration.json (controls, primary_endpoint, failure_conditions, seeds, budgets), registration_c.json (decision, seeds_rule, adoption_rule, predictions), amendment_3.json and amendment_4.json

main.jsonl: counted run purposes and CPU after the record registration_c (idx 2196); all 13 purposes match ^(search|gate|confirm):c\d+: and no run before idx 2196 matches; no duplicate run keys in the ledger
main.jsonl: compared spent_by for processes a and b (3576.0 and 13672.8 CPU-s) with the run purposes; the start-version runs (43.6 and 142.2 CPU-s) are not in it

dev_ledger.jsonl: listed every target:* and memory:* run with budget, CPU and scores; recomputed matched CPU = cpu(primary run) + share_per_run for all 7 matched records (14 pairs) and compared with the recorded reached flags: all agree
dev_ledger.jsonl: c:frozen keys == frozen keys and c:skills keys == skills keys in target_done; regex sum x 0.002 = 23.362906 equals the recorded spend of c:compute

WORK/t_checks.py: main() of targets.py on copies of the dev ledger with environments.load and run.Cache stubbed (no adapter loaded, no run): 8 scenarios for fewer_than_drawn, replacements, --dev 0 and a second start with another list
WORK/t_prefix.py: main() on two prefixes of main.jsonl (2196 and 3400 records) with the same stubs

WORK/t_matched.py: matched() with a fake cache and ledger on 8 synthetic CPU models (linear, overhead plus linear, flat, flat with noise, plateau then linear, square root, search arm, zero share), a second start, and a zero base budget
WORK/t_memory.py: repeated memory_of for generation 0 on forecasting and jobshop (source categories, 11.6 CPU-s) on a copy of the dev ledger and compared the resulting key with the dev ledger

findings.what: The check of the admitted list accepts wrong lists. With "fewer_than_drawn" set, any subset of the target categories passes, including one category or none. Duplicates are not rejected (targets = sorted(listed["admitted"]), no set). Nothing checks that the list covers every category whose effective role is target.
findings.why_it_matters: Amendment 4 fixes the target set: four categories with genassign, or the three admitted ones if genassign fails its audit. The unlock is irreversible and the primary endpoint is a mean over categories, so a list that drops a category (for example satisfiability, where the auditor expects 0 for every arm) changes the registered result. This check is the only code-level defence. It needs a wrong targets.json to trigger.
findings.evidence: WORK/t_checks.py, non-dev mode on copies of the dev ledger, run.Cache stubbed. {"admitted": ["satisfiability"], "fewer_than_drawn": true} -> PASSED CHECKS, appended {"type":"unlock","role":"target","targets":["satisfiability"]}. {"admitted": [], "fewer_than_drawn": true} -> PASSED CHECKS, unlock with targets []; the real driver would then fail at mean() on an empty list (line 91) after the unlock. Line 208: the count is only tested when 'short' is falsy. Duplicates: from reading only, not run.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute the expected set from the ledger: every category with effective role target that has an adapter in environments.REGISTRY. Require the admitted list to equal it, with no duplicates and at least one entry. For the short case require the file to name each missing target and the reason, require exactly N_TARGET minus that number, and write that into the unlock record. Do all of this before appending anything.

findings.what: The replace record is appended before the list is validated, and neither side of a replacement is checked. A start that is then refused leaves the record in the append-only ledger. A reserve on which the learner has already run can become a target. A category that is not a target can be named as replaced.
findings.why_it_matters: A refused start can change the registered ledger permanently: the replaced category has role 'dropped' from then on, and line 203 will never write a corrected record for it. The sealed-target rule (no learner run on a target before the test) can be broken by naming tour or colouring, which the external gate has used. A source category named as replaced leaves the pool and changes the memory of the skills arms.
findings.evidence: WORK/t_checks.py. (1) admitted [facility, routing, satisfiability] with replacements [{replaced: routing, reserve: genassign}] -> SystemExit 'the admitted list must be the 4 categories...', yet the replace record was appended; effective_role(routing) is now 'dropped', genassign 'target'. (2) After reassign/unlock/release of tour as adoption:4 (what external.py:104-128 writes), replacements [{replaced: flowshop, reserve: tour}] with admitted [facility, routing, satisfiability, tour] -> PASSED CHECKS, unlock written, effective_role(tour) == 'target'. (3) replacements [{replaced: binpacking, reserve: genassign}] -> PASSED CHECKS; binpacking is 'dropped', flowshop still 'target' and unlisted.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate first, append after. For each replacement require effective_role(replaced) == 'target' and effective_role(reserve) == 'reserve', and that the ledger holds no run on the reserve's category. Compute the roles the list would have with the replacements applied in memory, run the list check on that, and only then append the replace records followed by the unlock.

findings.what: Nothing enforces 'run once' or ties a later start to the list recorded at the unlock. A second start with a different targets.json passes the checks and measures on the new list. Every start appends the matched records again, and every completed start appends another target_done. report.py uses the last target_done (line 186) and the last matched record per arm (lines 242-243).
findings.why_it_matters: Amendment 3 says the target test is run once for all processes. After results are seen, a restart with a shorter list (allowed by fewer_than_drawn) would silently produce a second target_done on other categories, and the report would use it. The unlock record would then contradict the target_done record. With an unchanged list the duplicates are identical and harmless.
findings.evidence: WORK/t_checks.py, last scenario: on a ledger whose unlock record says ['facility','genassign','routing','satisfiability'], a start with {"admitted": ["facility","routing"], "fewer_than_drawn": true} -> PASSED CHECKS. WORK/t_matched.py: a second call of matched() on the same cache ran 0 new jobs and appended a second, identical matched record ('matched records now 2 | identical True'). Lines 131 and 252 append unconditionally.
findings.suggested_fix: If an unlock record of role target exists, require its 'targets' to equal the current list and stop otherwise. If a target_done record exists, stop with a message unless its targets, seeds and arm keys equal what this start computes, and never append a second one. Append a matched record only if none with the same arm and keys exists.

findings.what: Outside my part, raised because question 2 asks whether the matched record is enough. The record is enough (keys, reached per pair, share_per_run), but report.py only counts and prints 'reached'. No comparison against a matched arm is voided when a control fell short, and the success part 'targets' uses 'c:self minus c:compute' without looking at matched['c:compute'].
findings.why_it_matters: registration.json, failure_conditions, last item: any comparison in which the control received less measured CPU than the arm it is compared with is void. If c:compute stops at the twelve-level cap below its matched CPU, the report would still score 'not behind the compute-matched arm', which decides part 3 of the success condition and prediction C4.
findings.evidence: report.py:242-243 builds {'share_per_run', 'reached': count, 'of': n} and line 551 prints it. Lines 314-315 compute 'behind' from c['c:self minus c:compute']['min_change'][0] alone. A search of report.py for 'void' finds nothing. I did not run report.py. Confidence: high that no voiding exists; I read only these sections and the search results.
findings.suggested_fix: In targets_section, for every comparison whose control is a matched arm, compute per pair cpu(control) against cpu(arm), and against cpu(arm) + share from the keys. Mark the comparison void if any pair of the control is below its arm (or if reached is not all true, whichever reading is registered), and make the success part and the predictions read None or 'void' in that case. It would also help if targets.py wrote the matched CPU per pair and the name of the reference arm into the matched record.

findings.what: "--dev 0" is treated as not dev everywhere (args.dev is 0, falsy), so the scratch-ledger refusal is skipped and the real unlock is written, but seeds become reg["seeds"]["target"][:0] = []. Separately, the refusal compares os.path.abspath, which does not resolve a symbolic link to main.jsonl or live.jsonl.
findings.why_it_matters: A development flag can write the unlock of the sealed targets into the registered ledger and then fail on an empty seed list. The unlock is correct in content if the list is right, so a later proper start still works; the harm is an unlock at a moment nobody intended.
findings.evidence: WORK/t_checks.py, scenario dev0_default_ledger (targets.LEDGER pointed at a copy, no --ledger argument, --dev 0): PASSED CHECKS, appended replace and unlock. With the real cache the next step is cache.get([]) and mean() of an empty list at line 147 (ZeroDivisionError). The symlink case is from reading only.
findings.suggested_fix: Test 'args.dev is not None' in all four places and reject --dev values below 1. Compare os.path.realpath, or os.path.samefile when the file exists.

findings.what: Three small deviations from reading (d) of amendment 4. (1) The factor aims at 1.1 times the matched CPU ('a tenth to spare'), not at what is needed. (2) When the last two levels show no rise in CPU the factor is 8; the text gives no such case, and the needed factor is then unbounded, which the text would cap at 64. (3) The loop of twelve counts the unraised base budget as a level, so there are at most eleven raises. Also, the minimum factor of 2 gives the control up to about twice the matched CPU.
findings.why_it_matters: All of these give the control more CPU or stop at most one level earlier, so they are conservative for the claims. They are still differences between code and registered text and should be stated with the result. The overshoot also roughly doubles the cost of the matched arms in the worst case.
findings.evidence: Line 126: (v2 + (1.1 * want[pair] - c2) / slope) / v2, and 'factor = 8.0 if slope <= 0'. Line 110: for _ in range(12), first pass at value = budget[field]. WORK/t_matched.py: linear model -> budgets 40, 80, 5120, 10240, final CPU 2560 for a matched CPU of 2000; search-arm model -> final 3278 for 2000; flat model -> 12 measurements, the first unraised. Dev ledger: reached CPU / matched CPU between 1.06 and 1.94 over the 14 pairs.
findings.suggested_fix: Either drop the 1.1 and use 64 for a non-positive slope, or keep the code and state the three points in the report as the implemented reading. Use range(13) if twelve raises are meant. Record the number of levels and the final budget per pair in the matched record.

findings.what: 'What a process spent' is counted differently for the first two processes and for process c. spent_by (a and b) sums the search records' cpu_used and the gate and confirm records' CPU; that leaves out the runs that measure the start version (purposes search:N:self:start). spent_by_process_c sums every run by purpose, start runs included.
findings.why_it_matters: The registered control is generation 0 given at least the CPU the self lineage spent on rounds and gates. For processes a and b the matched arms are matched to about 1% less than that, and 'reached' is judged against the smaller number. The effect is small and usually covered by the overshoot, but the two rules differ without a stated reason.
findings.evidence: main.jsonl: spent_by for a = 1499.3 + 1542.4 + 42.4 + 197.3 + 44.2 + 250.5 = 3576.0 CPU-s (dev record: 7.151968 = 0.002 x 3576.0); runs with purposes search:1:self:start and search:2:self:start add 36.4 + 7.2 = 43.6 CPU-s (1.2%). For b: 13672.8 counted, search:b1:self:start 142.2 (1.0%) not counted. For c the regex includes search:c1:start (342.5 CPU-s).
findings.suggested_fix: Add the start runs of the self lineage to spent_by (runs with purpose '<tag>:start' for the counted search tags), or state the difference in the report.

findings.what: The freeze checks hold only for the ledger file that is given, and any path is accepted outside the development mode. A copy that ends before the record registration_c passes the checks and gets the unlock. The default is main.jsonl, while external.py and recursion.py default to live.jsonl; nothing checks that live.jsonl is not ahead of the ledger used. The record of amendment 4, whose readings this code implements, is not required either.
findings.why_it_matters: The target test could be started on a stale checkpoint before process c is frozen, on a fork of the chain. If main.jsonl is synchronised after external.py and recursion.py then writes to live.jsonl, the two files diverge and cannot be merged. Two drivers appending to one file at the same time would also break the chain (Ledger.append numbers records from its in-memory list). All of this needs an operator mistake.
findings.evidence: WORK/t_prefix.py: first 2196 records of main.jsonl (freeze of a and b present, registration_c absent) -> PASSED CHECKS, appended ['replace', 'unlock']. First 3400 records -> SystemExit 'process c is registered and not finished', nothing appended. external.py:65 and recursion.py:56 use default=LIVE; targets.py:180 uses default=LEDGER.
findings.suggested_fix: Outside --dev, accept only main.jsonl or live.jsonl, and stop if the other of the two exists and is not a prefix of (or equal to) the one used. Require the amendment records 3 and 4 that the registry directory holds to be in the ledger. Take an exclusive lock file for the duration of the run.

findings.what: The memory arms. 'earlier' is every category in the source pool now, in alphabetical order, one acquisition each at seed 1. external.py:128 releases tour and colouring into the pool only if the external gate ran, so the memory of skills, memory, b:skills, b:memory and c:memory has 11 categories after an adoption by process c and 9 otherwise. In the dev run the memory arms collapse.
findings.why_it_matters: The registered arms of the first two processes depend on the outcome of process c. The collapse is behaviour of the frozen learner, not of targets.py: learner.py:414-424 always recalls an entry (same >= score starts at 0; ties go to the last entry, so alphabetical order decides) and transfer.blend is 1.0, so weights learned on another category replace the starting weights. The predictions that memory does not help would be met for that reason, which the report should say.
findings.evidence: Dev ledger idx 3581: target:skills binpacking, memory_in 2, acquired 0.0 on all 24 fresh instances and train_acquired 0.0, untrained 0.9243, report 'transferred': true, held_back keys [29676.5, 1.0]; frozen on the same run: 0.9875. Dev log: skills 0.1820 against frozen 0.8360, b:skills 0.1441 against 0.8206, c:memory 0.0000. The dev memory held 2 entries (forecasting, jobshop); the real one will hold 9 or 11, so the size of the effect may differ.
findings.suggested_fix: State in the report how many categories the memory held and why. If the registered arms of the first two processes should not depend on process c, exclude categories released after the freeze of those processes from 'earlier'. Record the list 'earlier' in target_done.

findings.what: Observations on the matched arms from the dev ledger. (1) The search arm's scores did not move at all with the test-time budget. (2) Measured CPU leaves out the scoring of the training instances, which also runs at the raised test budget. (3) Matched arms of different processes share records, so a record's purpose does not name the arm. (4) In the matched record the field 'spent_by_self_lineage' also holds the spend of all four techniques of process c.
findings.why_it_matters: (1) The plain-search control is as registered, but in the dev run it burns CPU in a local search that has already converged, so 'not behind c:search' says little; the report should say so if the targets show the same. (2) The real cost of the search arm is about 1.67 times what is recorded (48 fresh plus 32 training answers against 48 timed). (3) The report must select by the keys in target_done, which it does. (4) Wording only.
findings.evidence: (1) idx 3587 and 3628: target:search binpacking at test_e 1.0 and 103.83, fresh_untrained lists identical, units 2,058,294 against 72,218,854; same for pmedian (idx 3588, 3629). (2) run.py:111-116: cpu_apply stops before the two scores(train_ids, ...) calls. (3) The matched record of c:compute has key a9e9f54f... for binpacking, whose run has purpose target:compute. (4) targets.py:131 and 250.
findings.suggested_fix: No change of code needed for (1) to (3); report (1) with the result and plan the wall time of c:search with (2) in mind. Rename the field to 'spent' or add 'process'.

findings.what: Checked and found correct: the definition of the process c arms, the counting of what process c spent, the reproducibility of the level sequence and of the memory on a second start, and the refusal before process c is frozen on a ledger that holds its registration.
findings.why_it_matters: These are the points the task asked to be attacked; the record of what was tried lets the next reviewer skip them.
findings.evidence: main.jsonl after idx 2196: 13 run purposes, all matching ^(search|gate|confirm):c\d+:, each run once (the gate of remeasure and combine reuses the runs of single; gate:c1:climb:incumbent is served from gate:c1:single:incumbent); 0 matching runs before idx 2196; external and recursion purposes do not match. Dev ledger: all 14 reached flags recomputed equal; alias arms have identical keys. WORK/t_matched.py: second start, 0 new runs. WORK/t_memory.py: recomputed key 9b0103c73c61 is in the dev ledger, 0 records appended. designs.default('a') has digest 4766c8e4..., the incumbent of gate:c1. A zero base budget would divide by zero at line 125, but the registered budgets are 40 and 1.
